subject: The glance/navigation reset — jump strip · dashboard tile row · card faces. Assessment of Paul's proposal to absorb the tile row's dynamic content into the card faces, plus answers to G-a (where ranking goes), G-c (the closed-card state), G-d (what sits under the strip).
review_level: flow / IA (zoom-out on the top-of-app architecture, not screen-component)
gate: NOTHING HERE EXECUTES. Every finding is a proposal. No file was edited. Two findings (F1, F9) argue AGAINST parts of what Paul described wanting — they are arguments, not vetoes.

what_this_review_does_with_it: No finding here rests on 'she does not respond to asks.' F7 (what sits under the strip) is argued ENTIRELY from the governing glance/repository principle and from measured layout cost, not from engagement.

The Fernwood candidate 'Among competing solicitation surfaces, demonstrated engagement sets altitude' (design-principles/fernwood.md, 2026-07-26) is NOT invoked anywhere in this review. Its whole evidence base is the retired record. Flagged for Paul in principles_to_propose §5.

My own prior pass today, F13 (the ribbon + 'OK sounds good'), had THREE grounds. Ground 2 was the 0-of-35 count. ⚠️ WITHDRAWN. F13 now stands on ground 1 (the ribbon's ratified job is attribution, not information) and ground 3 (the promise has no delivery) only — both of which are independent of engagement and both of which I still hold.

The strip's 5-of-5 is used ONLY as a design stance ('the strip moves her and must not become an ask'), never as proof about her willingness. Its provenance caveat stands: those events fired from Paul's device.

MECHANISM facts survive and ARE used: the queue renders one card at a time behind 'Another question ›' (measured at 12146-12152 + 12792 — MAX_VISIBLE=5 caps the SET, `idx` renders ONE, every offer carries position 0), so the effective visible set is 1, not 5; card_expanded fires from a subset of the writers that open cards.

user_context.primary_user: Mom, at Fernwood — resident steward, 414 x 848, A+ text, one-handed, half-engaged, on the frozen instance. Secondary and binding: a first-time household owner at a near-empty estate (Paul's own condo walk), who meets the same top-of-app architecture with 1-4 populated modules instead of 13.
core_jobs_to_be_done: Tell me what is worth knowing about my place right now, without me assembling it.
Get me to the thing I came for (the Journal, the rain, the sky) in one move.
Let me tell you what I am seeing, at the moment I am looking at it.
user_context.context_of_use: Phone, in bed or on the porch, seconds not minutes, at A+ text on a 414px column. The page is 16 cards long. Sessions in the record run 13-91 seconds.
assumptions_made: That the consolidation is being designed for BOTH instances at once (Fernwood-full and a near-empty household), because the engine renders both from one template. Stated because a decision that is right for 13 populated cards can be wrong for 2.

That 'her conditions' (414 x 848, A+) govern every layout judgement here. I did NOT run the browser harness for this review — this is a source read. Every pixel claim below is arithmetic from sourced CSS lines and is marked as such.
That Paul's proposal is a design intent to be assessed, not a decision already made. He asked whether it loses anything.

An ask-card's answer must be reachable without scrolling, at HER conditions (fernwood.md, candidate 2026-08-24)
Nielsen #1 visibility of system status · #6 recognition over recall · #8 aesthetic and minimalist design
Norman — signifiers, and the cost of removing one without replacing the affordance it advertised
the_headline: ⭐ THE TILE ROW IS NOT A DUPLICATE LAYER. It is FOUR JOBS wearing one component, and only ONE of them is duplicated. Paul is right that the summary text repeats — that redundancy is real, it is measurably harmful (it is occurrence 4 of 'One engine, one verdict'), and deleting the second slot deletes the second engine by construction rather than by maintenance. But while the row was summarising it was also (2) the ONLY above-the-fold door to four cards the jump strip does not name, (3) the host of the loop's invitation lens, and (4) the only place where the domains sit close enough together to be compared in one look. 'Consolidating without losing anything' is TRUE of the job he was looking at and FALSE of the three he was not. The consolidation is safe if and only if those three get named destinations BEFORE the row is deleted — and all three have cheap answers.

findings.observation: The jump strip and the tile row are NOT the same six things. Strip (6535-6542): Weather · Vehicles · Equipment · Household Systems · Gardening · Wildlife. Tile row tier A (6657-6688): Weather · Plants · Wildlife · Sky & Stars · Fishing · Journal; tier B (6697-6704): Vehicles · Property. Measured overlap is four. FOUR CARDS ARE REACHABLE ABOVE THE FOLD ONLY FROM A TILE: Fishing (card 9 of 16), Sky & Stars (10), Journal (11), Property (12). Absorb the tile row and their only door becomes a scroll past eight or more full cards at A+ on a 414px column. ⚠️ The code already records this exact defect being FIXED: the Journal tile's own comment (6677-6684) says it is 'the MOST-OPENED card in the app (41 of 139 expansions) sitting 8th of 13 with no tile of its own, so the only way to reach the thing she asked for was to scroll past seven cards.' Paul's proposal, executed literally, restores that state for Journal and adds three more.
findings.user_impact: The job 'get me to the thing I came for in one move' fails for four domains, including the one she asked for by name and the one she opens most. She does not lose information — the cards still exist — she loses the ability to REACH them without a hunt, at the exact conditions (A+, one hand, seconds) where a hunt is what makes her close the app.
findings.principle_invoked: Norman — removing a signifier removes the affordance's advertisement even though the affordance survives; Nielsen #6 recognition rather than recall. Also Fernwood 'Make every surface read at half-engagement.'
findings.recommendation: Do not delete the tile row's NAVIGATION job — TRANSFER it, per domain, and make the transfer explicit rather than implied. Three transfer routes already exist or are cheap: (a) JOURNAL is already covered — 'Look back ›' lives in the Almanac card head (6563-6564), and Paul ALREADY made exactly this substitution on 2026-09-07 beat 3 when he removed the Journal tile for a household 'because the composer card already carries Look back ›.' That precedent is the model: name the replacement door, then delete. (b) SKY, FISHING and PROPERTY have no such door — they need one, and the cheapest is F2's additive second strip row. (c) Anything with no transfer route is a deliberate demotion to scroll-only and must be RULED, not defaulted into. ⛔ The falsifier for the whole consolidation: after it ships, every card that had a tile must be reachable in one tap from above the fold, or its demotion is written down as a decision.

findings.observation: After the collapse the jump strip is the app's ONLY index, and it indexes 6 of 16 cards — 37.5%. Measured card stream at HEAD: weather(1) vehicles(2) equipment(3) household(4) plants(5) turf(6) weeds(7) wildlife(8) fishing(9) celestial(10) fieldnotes/Journal(11) property(12) candidates(13) references(14) place-log(15) release-notes(16). An index that omits ten of sixteen destinations is not an index; it is a shortcut list that happens to sit where an index goes. Today that is tolerable because the tile row covers four more and the reader can see the rest as she scrolls past their tiles. Remove the row and the omission becomes load-bearing.
findings.user_impact: Recognition-over-recall collapses. She must remember that Fishing exists and that it is somewhere below Wildlife. For the household owner with 2 populated modules the failure is different but worse: `applyModuleTiles` (18456-18461) hides a strip link unless its module is `populated`, so a strip that already covers 6 of 16 can render as two links.
findings.principle_invoked: Rosenfeld/Morville — an index's value is coverage plus stable position. Cross-project 'A menu's order is a PLACE.' The strip is the menu; a menu that names a third of the rooms is the problem the tile row was quietly patching.
findings.recommendation: Re-scope strip membership as PART OF the consolidation, in the same change, ADDITIVELY. ⛔ Do NOT reorder or edit the existing six: they are Mom's own five categories in her own order, confirmed by her 2026-08-03, and the template's own comment (6532-6534) says reordering her list 'is the same act as rewording household systems, which this app has already done to her once.' The safe form is a SECOND ROW beneath her six — Sky & Stars · Fishing · Journal · Property (or whichever survive F1's transfer test) — visually subordinate (smaller, or unglyphed), her six untouched and unmistakably first. ⭐ This also satisfies the brief's binding constraint: a strip row of destinations MOVES her and does not ASK her, so growing the strip this way cannot spend the one thing on this product that works. ⚠️ It does grow the strip's height: at A+ (17px, 44px min target, 8px gap, 4206-4223) a second two-column row costs ~52px, which the tile row's deletion returns many times over.

findings.observation: The 'Worth a look' prompt (18626-18637, `dash-plant-check`, wired by `wirePlantCheckPrompt` to the composer, NOT to the card — Paul's call 2026-07-14) is the one tile row that does something a card face structurally cannot: it is a tap target inside the glance whose destination is a capture surface. A `.main-card-header` is itself the card's open control (6712-6718), so a nested target with a different destination inside it is an affordance collision and an accessibility one. ⭐ Extending my prior pass (F6): this is not merely a stray control. It is lens 1 of the ratified temporal-lens contract — 'The ask (today, curated) … the loop's invitation lens' [paul-ratified 2026-08-31] — and it is strand 3 of the governing principle, the flywheel. Deleting the tile row without re-siting it does not move a feature; it removes a ratified member of a three-grain contract and the loop's only invitation at the glance altitude.
findings.user_impact: The glance stops being an exchange and becomes a broadcast. The one moment the app says 'here is something to go look at, and tell me what you see' — pairing a fresh, specific, near-horizon signal with a one-tap way to answer it — has no other home in the product.
findings.principle_invoked: CLAUDE.md governing principle, strand 3 (the loop / the flywheel). Fernwood 'The temporal-lens contract' — lenses 1 and 2 are one lens at two altitudes and both read `carePeakToday()`; deleting one altitude is a change to a ratified contract, not a layout tidy.
findings.recommendation: Site it in the ONE synthesis line (F5), not in a card header. 'Worth a look · the clematis · note it ›' is exactly the shape of a synthesis phrase, it is already computed by the same `carePeakToday()` engine the card face will use (so it is a projection, not a fifth engine), and the line is not a role=button — a link inside it is legal where a link inside a header is not. Fallback if Paul rules the synthesis line out: my prior F6 stands — the closed face STATES it flatly with no control, and the tap moves to the first row of the open Plants card body. ⚠️ Paul's ruling is needed on one thing: this places an invitation-shaped element near the strip, and the brief's constraint is that the strip must not become an ask. My read is that it is safe — it invites her to LOOK AT HER PROPERTY, not to answer a question about the app, and it routes to the composer she reached for unprompted — but it is his call, not mine, and the mitigation if he wants one is a clear visual break between the strip and the line.

findings.observation: The density arithmetic, measured from the renderers. A dash cell is a multi-row block: WEATHER renders condition+temp+H/L, then the station-vs-grid 7-day rain row, then up to 3 alert rows, then '+N more' — up to 6 rows (18560-18614). PLANTS renders up to 2 'Worth a look' rows, then an 'At their peak' block containing ONE ROW PER PLANT at peak, then the month breadcrumb (18620-18674). WILDLIFE renders birds + arriving-this-week + leaving-this-week + amphibians — up to 4 (18715-18722). SKY renders moon + sunset (with the terrain 'last light here' clause) + next event — 3 (18753-18793). FISHING renders verdict + window + phase + lake temp in one row (18735-18741). That is roughly TWENTY rows of tease across eight cells. The receiving slot, `.main-card-summary`, is a single prose element: 14px / 17.5px at A+, line-height 1.45, no clamp (1671, 6325). Structurally it can wrap, but a header that wraps to five lines has stopped being a header.
findings.user_impact: Roughly twenty rows must become roughly eight one-line faces. That is a real editorial cut and it will be made by whoever writes the code unless it is ruled first. Named casualties, in the order I would fight for them: (1) the STATION-VS-GRID 7-day rain figure — the number Mom disbelieved on 2026-07-26 and was right about by 14x, whose renderer carries a comment saying 'a measured signal must never be silently replaced by a modelled one on the glance' (18570-18581); (2) the alerts; (3) the per-plant peak LIST, which becomes a count or a truncation and a count is not a read; (4) the bird arriving/leaving week callouts, the only week-grain signal in Wildlife; (5) the 'last light here' terrain line, which is the single most place-specific sentence on the glance.
findings.principle_invoked: Ordering first, then type in service of it — 'surfacing data of unequal importance through a uniform component' is named in its When-it-applies. Source-hierarchy drives layout, which is what protects the measured rain figure specifically.
findings.recommendation: Rule the cut BEFORE the build, item by item, and record each as kept / moved-into-the-card / deleted. My recommendation per item: the rain figure MOVES INTO the card at the top of the rainfall panel where it can carry its own provenance (a one-line face cannot), and its measured/modelled distinction is NOT allowed to survive as an unlabelled number on any face. Alerts: weather is the one card permitted a conditional second line, and only for the single highest-ranked alert. Peak list: the face names the count AND up to two names ('Three at their peak — hydrangea, deutzia'), never a bare count. Week callouts and 'last light here': into the card. ⛔ The rule that makes this safe: nothing may be deleted as a side effect of a layout change — a thing either has a named new home or an explicit decision that it goes.

findings.observation: G-a names the loss as RANKING. It is bigger than that: it is ADJACENCY. Eight cells in a two-column grid put weather, plants, wildlife, sky, fishing and the journal inside one visual field, so a reader compares them in one look. Distribute the same content to sixteen card faces and — measured against the card geometry at A+ — no two summaries are ever on screen together. The reader cannot compare because the comparison now costs a scroll, and a gap the eye must cross costs precision. Ranking is the part of comparison that a machine can do for her; adjacency is the part she was doing herself, for free, and it is the part nobody is proposing to replace.
findings.user_impact: 'Tell me what is worth knowing about my place right now' becomes 'scan sixteen card faces and assemble the read yourself' — which is the assemble-it-yourself burden the glance layer exists to remove, repacked vertically instead of spatially.
findings.principle_invoked: Lead with the synthesis, not the rows — and note its own Avoid clause cuts BOTH ways here: 'assuming spatial compression equals synthesis; it doesn't.' The tile row was compression-mistaken-for-synthesis, so deleting it is right; but the answer is a real synthesis, not the absence of both. Also 'Juxtapose large differences; superpose small ones' — a gap the eye must cross costs precision.
findings.recommendation: ⭐ I hold my prior recommendation (d) and now consider it load-bearing rather than preferred: ONE synthesis line where the tile grid is today. One or two sentences naming only what is UNUSUAL today, each phrase linked to the card that holds it, cap two phrases, every phrase a PROJECTION of a card's own resolver and never a new claim, absent entirely on a day with nothing notable. The mechanism is already built and ratified — `MOM_ACK_DATA.links = [{phrase, card}]`, many phrases each linked, and a phrase no longer in the message is skipped rather than rendered as a dead control (standing rule 2). Reuse that vocabulary; do not mint a state. It restores exactly one place where items compete, at the smallest size the product can spend, and it is the only proposal on the table that answers G-a without touching card order or putting a status dot on the strip. Falsifier: if the line ever says something no card face says, it has become a fifth engine and must be cut back.

findings.observation: `.dash-cell.dash-imagery` (3715-3723) renders the aerial photograph as the Property tile's background with the title and sub reversed out over a dark gradient. It is the only image above the cards and the only place on the glance where the reader SEES the property rather than reading about it. Its own provenance: a ux-expert recommendation of 2026-05-27, 'absorb the Property card with a visual lead so Mom can SEE the surface before tapping' (3684-3687). A card-face summary line cannot carry it; text is not a substitute for a picture of your own land.
findings.user_impact: The glance loses its only visceral element. In Norman's terms the top of the app becomes entirely behavioral and reflective with nothing visceral in it — which for a field-journal product whose whole promise is 'looking out at the land' is a real cost even though nothing stops working.
findings.principle_invoked: Content and function first, form follows — and then form has to be excellent (cross-project, paul-stated). Norman, Emotional Design — the visceral layer. Fernwood's founding tone: 'looking out at the land, not a to-do list.'
findings.recommendation: Two honest options and I recommend the first. (a) The image moves to the Property CARD as a header-width lead inside the card, and the glance accepts the loss — clean, and the card is where depth belongs under the governing principle. ⚠️ State the consequence plainly: Property is card 12 of 16 with no strip link, so under F1/F2 unremedied this effectively deletes the image from the product. It only works if Property gets a strip entry. (b) The app keeps exactly ONE image above the cards and it is this one, as a single full-width band under the synthesis line. More striking, and it re-introduces a fixed element above the fold that has to earn its height every day — which it cannot, because it never changes, which makes it furniture by the F8 test. I would not do (b).

findings.observation: G-d, answered. Measured DOM order at HEAD: header → jump strip (6535) → Fernwood Almanac composer card (6559) → Mama's Perspective master card (6623) → dash-strip tile row (6655) → the sixteen cards (6711+). So today the tile row — the glance — is ALREADY buried under two capture surfaces, and if it is absorbed, the two capture surfaces sit directly under the strip with the glance now distributed below them. That is the wrong answer to G-d, and the reason has nothing to do with engagement: the governing principle's strand 1 says the glance is the near-horizon decision read and it LEADS. Neither the composer nor the confirm queue is a glance. Both are capture. The freshest, most decision-changing material in the app (today's conditions, what is at peak, tonight's sky) is sitting below two surfaces whose content does not change with the weather.
findings.user_impact: The first thing the app shows after the door is a blank text field and a question. The reader has to get past two authoring surfaces to reach anything about her place. At 414 x A+ the arithmetic is unkind: the Almanac card (head + a 2-row textarea + the full-width action button) plus the Mama's Perspective master (head + summary + acknowledgment + one confirm card, ledgered at ~638px on 2026-08-24) put the first live content well past one screen height of 848px. The 08-24 candidate already ruled the shape of this: 'the finding is the position, not the height — a card that is 75% of a screen is fine first and wrong third.'
findings.principle_invoked: CLAUDE.md governing principle, strand 1 (the glance leads). Freshness sets altitude — 'live and decision-changing material leading.' Fernwood candidate 'Give before you ask' (used here as an EXCHANGE argument about ordering, not as an engagement claim). ⛔ NOT invoked: 'demonstrated engagement sets altitude' — that candidate's evidence base is the record Paul retired tonight, and this finding does not need it.
findings.recommendation: Under the strip goes the GLANCE: the synthesis line (F5), then the first live cards in the reader's own order. The four-card input stack moves as ONE BLOCK to below the glance and above the reference cards. ⚠️ Three constraints. (1) This does not reopen W8·a — 'four separate main cards' stays exactly as ratified 2026-07-30; only the block's position moves, which is one splice, not a restructure. (2) The acknowledgment ribbon (`#mp-summary`, 6640) is the give-back and Paul's own note says it 'surfaces stuff she will wanna look at,' so it travels with the block — if he wants the receipt to stay high, that is a SEPARATE ruling and it means splitting the master card, which W8·a deliberately fused. My recommendation is: move the block whole, do not split it. (3) ⭐ The strongest argument for this move is the strip itself: a reader who navigates by the strip never sees what sits between the strip and the cards, so that slot is spent entirely on the reader who SCROLLS — and the scrolling reader is precisely the one the glance exists for. Putting capture there spends the glance's slot on someone who is not looking for capture.

findings.observation: G-c, detailed. My prior pass gave a six-type grammar for what a closed card says; what it did not give is the DEGRADATION LADDER Paul is asking for, or a way to tell an honest line from furniture without an argument. The five static faces are the live case: Vehicles reads 'The machines we keep — and what each one needs', References 'The back pages — specs, sources, and records', Property 'Land · Sky · History'. Every one of them is true, well written, and identical on every visit — which is the 2026-08-04 definition of furniture that got the Mama's Perspective framing line removed.
findings.user_impact: A face that describes the card answers the wrong question. The reader is not asking 'what is this card about' — she learned that on visit two. She is asking 'is there anything new behind this door?' A permanent sentence answers the first question every day and the second one never, so she learns to skip the face, and then the faces that DO carry news get skipped with them.
findings.principle_invoked: Fernwood 'Make every surface read at half-engagement.' Cross-project 'A design rule must be a claim someone can check — if it cannot be violated, it is decoration' (this is what the falsifier below is for). Nielsen #8, aesthetic and minimalist design: every extra unit of information competes with the units that matter.
findings.recommendation: ⭐ THE JOB, stated once: a closed card's line answers 'is there anything new behind this door?', never 'what is this card about?' ⭐ THE LADDER — evaluated in order, first non-null wins, and a resolver never falls back to a rung it cannot honestly fill: (1) THE LIVE LINE — the domain's current verdict in its own words, measured value leading, modelled word following in the same sentence. (2) THE DATED CHANGE — no live signal but a dated record exists: 'Last touched: Bolores, RetroSound, Aug 9', derived from `serviceHistory`, which already carries stable ids and dates. This is the only thing about a reference card that can ever be new. (3) THE CHARACTER LINE — no live signal and no dated record, but an honest fact that is true of TODAY and changes over the year: 'Pruning and inspecting this September.' (4) ABSENCE — title only. No dash, no ellipsis, no placeholder, no 'Nothing here yet.' ⭐ THE FURNITURE FALSIFIER, and it is mechanically checkable, which is what makes rung 3 safe: RENDER THE RESOLVER AT TODAY+30 DAYS. If the string is identical, it is furniture and must degrade to rung 4. That converts Paul's 08-04 word into a build assertion. ⚠️ Loading sits OUTSIDE the ladder: my prior F4 stands — fetching and nothing-to-say must never print the same string, and there is exactly ONE fetching string in the build. ⛔ AND A BOUNDARY I want stated so the empty ruling is not over-applied: 'better to not display something than display something empty' governs the SUMMARY SLOT, not the card. A card whose body holds `.empty-invite` (18400-18423) is not empty — it is holding deliberate first-visit content for a new household. Reading the ruling as 'hide empty cards' would delete a household's entire first screen.

findings.observation: G-a, the ranking half — assessed as a design proposition only. ⭐ THE FACT THAT DECIDES IT: card order is ALREADY dynamic, and it is already ranked BY THE READER. `orderCardsByRanking()` (18186-18203) reorders the card stream by `READER_RANKING`, the order the reader gave at onboarding, under a comment that is a direct quote: 'THE RANKING DECIDES THE ORDER [paul-stated 2026-09-06]: we are building it based on this input that you provided us. A person who put Gardening first found it fifth.' The app then SAYS SO on the card face — `emptyCardSource()` (18204-18212) renders 'You put Gardening first.' At Fernwood the same thing is true by a different channel: the strip's six are Mom's own five categories in her own order, confirmed by her 2026-08-03, and page order was reordered to MATCH the strip on 2026-08-04 because 'a nav whose order fights the page is disorienting.' So on BOTH instances the card order is a reader-declared PLACE. Frequency-ranking does not fill an empty slot — it OVERWRITES a declared order with an inferred one, on the same axis, eleven days after that axis was ruled.
findings.user_impact: What a reader experiences if card order moves under her between visits, four effects, all of them cumulative: (1) RECALL DIES. Position is the only wayfinding on a 16-card page at A+; if position is a ranking it is supposed to move, so every visit costs a full scan — exactly the cost an index exists to remove. (2) THE RANKING MEASURES ITS OWN OUTPUT. A card near the top is opened more BECAUSE it is near the top; frequency then confirms the position that caused it. This is rich-get-richer, it locks in within a few visits, and the bottom of the list becomes permanently invisible. The product has already run this experiment on a different surface: the confirm queue renders ONE card at a time and every offer carries `position: 0` (12792), and the result was one card holding the head for three weeks as the only card seen — a fact about the surface, not about her. Frequency-ranked cards is the same mechanism with a slower clock. (3) THE STRIP AND THE PAGE DIVERGE ON DAY ONE. The strip order is fixed; a frequency-ordered page drifts away from it immediately, which reverses the 2026-08-04 decision by name and puts the one affordance that works into disagreement with the page it points at. (4) IT SILENTLY CONTRADICTS THE APP'S OWN SENTENCE. The face says 'You put Gardening first' on a card that frequency has moved to fourth. That is a provenance lie about the reader's own words.
findings.principle_invoked: ⛔ Cross-project, paul-ratified: 'A menu's order is a PLACE; a worklist's order is a RANKING — never let one set the other. The tell: a row that moves when an unrelated item closes.' Plus standing rule 5's caveat — changeable is the message to her, not a licence for churn; a change must be journey-aware, and this one reverses a nine-day-old ruling.
findings.recommendation: ⭐ RECOMMEND AGAINST frequency-ranked card order. This is an argument, not a veto. And the underlying instinct is right and worth keeping, so here is where the frequency signal SHOULD go, in order of my preference: (a) FREQUENCY RANKS THE SYNTHESIS LINE, NOT THE CARDS. The line (F5) is the one place where competing is correct — it is a worklist by construction, it is two phrases, and it moves every day without moving anything the reader navigates by. This is the ratified rule applied exactly: the ranking goes in the worklist, the index stays a place. (b) FREQUENCY PROPOSES A CHANGE TO THE DECLARED ORDER AND SHE RATIFIES IT. 'You open Weather most — want it first?' The order then remains reader-declared, stays stable between visits, and the reader learns that her ordering is hers and changeable, which is standing rule 5 doing real work rather than being asserted. ⚠️ This is an ask, so it is authored content and Paul's gate. (c) FREQUENCY IS MEASUREMENT ONLY, feeding the backlog, changing nothing on screen. ⚠️ AND ONE DEPENDENCY WHOEVER RULES THIS MUST KNOW, though the measurement design is the researcher's lane not mine: my prior pass measured SEVEN writers of `.expanded` on a `.main-card` and only TWO emit `card_expanded`; two of the silent ones fire without a tap at all, so they can never appear in an open-rate denominator. A frequency ordering computed on that counter would rank the cards by an instrument that cannot see most of the opens.

findings.observation: Unprompted, my lane. `applyModuleTiles()` applies THREE different visibility rules to one module state and the consolidation makes the mismatch bite. Cards hide only when the module is `off` (18430-18432). Tiles hide unless the module is `populated` (18434-18436). Strip links hide unless the target card's module is `populated` (18456-18461). So a module that is ON but EMPTY — which is the normal state of a brand-new household's ranked interests — renders a CARD with an invitation in it, and NO tile and NO strip link. The card face then says 'You put Gardening first' (18208) about a card the app's own navigation refuses to link to.
findings.user_impact: For the first-time owner this is the worst-hit case, because at a new estate MOST modules are on-and-empty. The app asks for a ranking, tells the reader it is using their ranking, and then omits the ranked-first module from the only index on the page. Today the tile row partially masks this because the reader scrolls past the tile grid and sees the shape of the app. After the collapse the strip is the whole index and the omission is total.
findings.principle_invoked: Nielsen #1 visibility of system status, and cross-project 'A value's provenance and freshness must be shown as honestly as the value itself' — an index that silently omits a destination the app has just promised is a status lie by omission.
findings.recommendation: Split the two questions the `populated` test is currently answering at once. NAVIGATION should key on PRESENCE, not on content: if a card is rendered, it is reachable from the index. CONTENT should key on `populated`: an empty module's strip entry links to a card whose face is absent (F8 rung 4) and whose body carries its invitation. That is honest in both directions — she can always reach what exists, and nothing pretends to hold news it does not have. ⛔ The alternative (keep hiding links for empty modules) is defensible ONLY if the card is hidden too, and that contradicts the ranked-interests design shipped 2026-09-06.

findings.observation: Unprompted, and created by tonight's ruling. `renderEmptyCards()` carries a shipped design decision whose stated rationale Paul retired hours ago. At 18403-18404: '⭐ THE ASK ONLY WHERE THERE IS SOMETHING OF THEIRS TO CONFIRM (content-steward 2026-09-06; the one measured reader is 0-for-35 on affordances that ask). Unranked cards sit quiet on one line.' The BEHAVIOUR may still be right — an ask on a card the reader never mentioned is arguably noise regardless of engagement data. But its written justification is now a retired prior, sitting in the engine as an authority the next reader will inherit.
findings.user_impact: No direct user impact today. The impact is on every future design decision that reads this comment and treats the 0-of-35 as settled evidence — which is precisely the failure CLAUDE.md names as this repo's most repeated one: a wrong SSOT row that nothing re-derives. The same number is quoted in other places I did not audit.
findings.principle_invoked: Cross-project 'A design rule must be a claim someone can check.' A rule whose evidence has been withdrawn is not checkable; it is inherited.
findings.recommendation: Two acts, and neither of them changes what renders. (1) Re-argue or withdraw the RATIONALE at 18403-18404. If the ask-gating is kept, keep it on a reason that survives — my proposal: 'an ask attached to a module the reader did not name has no ground to stand on', which is about relevance rather than about her. (2) ⛔ SWEEP FOR THE NUMBER. `grep` for '0-for-35' / '0 of 35' / '35 offered' across viewer.html, engine/, the plans and the principle libraries, and mark each site retired-as-evidence rather than deleting it — the count is a true fact about a frozen prototype and it should stay legible as history. I did not run that sweep; it touches files I am not permitted to edit, and it is a decision about the record, not a design call.

direct_answers.Q1_does_his_proposal_lose_nothing: No — it loses four things, and one of them is a regression of a defect this repo already fixed and documented. What it genuinely loses: (1) F1/F2 — the only above-the-fold door to Fishing, Sky & Stars, Journal and Property, none of which the jump strip names. (2) F3 — the loop's invitation lens, a ratified member of the temporal-lens contract, which cannot legally live inside a card header. (3) F5 — adjacency, i.e. the ability to compare domains in one look, which is a bigger loss than the ranking G-a names. (4) F6 — the aerial image, the only visual of the property above the cards. What it genuinely WINS, and I want this on the record because it is real: it deletes the second weather engine by construction rather than by maintenance (occurrence 4 of 'One engine, one verdict', whose own text says the answer to a fourth is that the two should have been one); it removes the tile-vs-card 'which do I tap' ambiguity; and it reclaims several hundred px above the first card at A+. ⭐ The verdict: DO IT, but not as a deletion. Do it as four transfers, three of which are cheap and one of which (the synthesis line) is the thing G-a is asking for anyway. 'Consolidating without losing anything' becomes TRUE if the transfers are named before the row is cut, and FALSE if the row is cut first.
direct_answers.Q2_what_sits_directly_under_the_strip: Not the two ask surfaces — the GLANCE. See F7. Recommended order under the strip: (1) the one synthesis line, present only when it has something to say; (2) the live cards in the reader's own declared order; (3) the four-card input stack, moved as one block, W8·a untouched; (4) the reference cards. The argument is the governing principle's strand 1 — the glance leads — plus the measured fact that at 414 x A+ the two capture cards push the first live content past one screen. ⛔ I am NOT arguing this from engagement, and I withdraw the engagement-based version of the argument per tonight's ruling. The sharpest supporting point is structural: a reader who navigates by the strip never sees what sits between the strip and the cards, so that slot is spent entirely on the reader who scrolls — and the scrolling reader is the one the glance exists for. ⚠️ One thing to rule with it: the acknowledgment ribbon travels with the block. If Paul wants the receipt to stay high, that means splitting the master card, which W8·a deliberately fused; my recommendation is to move the block whole.
direct_answers.Q3_what_a_closed_card_says: See F8 for the full ladder. In one paragraph: the closed line's job is to answer 'is there anything new behind this door?', never 'what is this card about?' — which is why the five static faces are wrong even though they are well written. Four rungs, first non-null wins, no falling back to a rung you cannot honestly fill: the live line → the dated change → the character line (true of today, changes over the year) → absence. Absence means the title alone: no dash, no ellipsis, no placeholder, no 'Nothing here yet.' Loading is outside the ladder and has exactly one string in the whole build. ⭐ The new piece this pass adds is the falsifier that makes rung 3 safe and Paul's 'furniture' word checkable: render the resolver at today+30; if the string is identical, it is furniture and degrades to rung 4. ⛔ And the boundary: the empty ruling governs the summary SLOT, not the card — a card holding a household's first-visit invitation is not empty.
direct_answers.Q4_ranking_card_order_by_access_frequenc: RECOMMEND AGAINST, as a design proposition — see F9, and note this is an argument, not a veto. The deciding fact is that card order is already ranked, by the READER: `orderCardsByRanking()` ships today under the ruling 'THE RANKING DECIDES THE ORDER [paul-stated 2026-09-06] — we are building it based on this input that you provided us', and at Fernwood the equivalent is Mom's own five categories in her order with page order matched to the strip in 2026-08-04. Frequency does not fill an empty slot; it overwrites a declared order with an inferred one on the same axis. What a reader would experience: recall dies, because position is the only wayfinding on a 16-card page; the ranking measures its own past output and locks in within a few visits (the confirm queue already ran this experiment — one card at position 0 held the head for three weeks); the strip and the page diverge on day one, putting the one working affordance in disagreement with the page it points at; and the app's own sentence 'You put Gardening first' starts contradicting where Gardening sits. Where the instinct SHOULD go: frequency ranks the SYNTHESIS LINE, which is a worklist by construction and is exactly where the ratified rule says a ranking belongs; or frequency PROPOSES a change to her declared order and she ratifies it, which keeps the order hers and stable and makes 'everything is changeable' do real work.
direct_answers.Q5_critical_in_my_own_lane_unprompted: Two, both graded critical by my own definition because they break the job rather than add friction to it, and both with code evidence at HEAD. (1) F1 — four cards lose their only above-the-fold door, and the Journal case is a documented regression: the code comment that created that tile says the pre-tile state was 'the only way to reach the thing she asked for was to scroll past seven cards.' (2) F2 — after the collapse the sole index covers 6 of 16 cards, and for a new household it can render as two links; an index that names a third of the rooms is not an index. Both are cheap to fix and both must be fixed IN the same change, not after it. ⛔ I do not rank these against other seats' findings and I do not decide. Also surfaced, at important: F10 (navigation hides links for a module the app has just told the reader it is prioritising) and F11 (a retired evidence claim is written into the engine as a shipped design rationale).

open_questions_for_user: F2 — do you accept an ADDITIVE second strip row (Sky · Fishing · Journal · Property), with Mom's six untouched and first? The alternative is ruling those four to scroll-only, which is defensible but must be a decision.

F3 — may the 'Worth a look' invitation live inside the synthesis line, directly under the strip? It routes to the composer, so it is invitation-shaped near the affordance you said must never become an ask. I read it as safe; it is your call.
F4 — the station-vs-grid 7-day rain figure: confirm it moves INTO the weather card with its provenance intact and does not survive as an unlabelled number on any face.
F5 — the synthesis line: one phrase or two, and does it live above the cards permanently or only when it has something to say? I recommend two-max, and only when it has something.
F6 — the aerial image: into the Property card and accept the glance loses it (my recommendation, conditional on Property getting a strip entry), or keep exactly one image above the cards?
F7 — does the four-card input stack move BELOW the glance as one block? And if so, does the acknowledgment ribbon travel with it, or do you want the master card split (which reverses part of W8·a)?
F8 — for Vehicles / Equipment / Household Systems / References / Property: rung 2 (last dated change) where a dated record exists, or rung 4 (absence)? I recommend rung 2 where available.
F9 — if you still want frequency to do work, which of the three placements: the synthesis line, a propose-and-ratify change to the declared order, or measurement only?
F11 — do you want the 0-of-35 sweep run across the corpus, marking each site retired-as-evidence rather than deleting it?
follow_up_research_suggested: The card-open denominator must be rebuilt before ANY frequency claim is argued — seven writers of `.expanded`, two emit `card_expanded`, two fire without a tap. This is the user-researcher's lane and F9(a)/(b) depend on it.

The '41 of 139 expansions' figure that justified the Journal tile comes from the same instrument and inherits the same defect. It is the strongest single piece of evidence behind F1 and it should be re-derived rather than re-quoted.

Once the tile row is gone, `jumpstrip_viewed` changes meaning — the strip becomes the only thing above the cards. Re-baseline before any strip claim, and the contested MOM-CYCLE-LOG readings (:1115 vs :1816) must be resolved first.

A one-question read, whenever a real reader meets the new closed faces: 'does this line tell you enough to decide whether to open it?' That is the only success test for the whole F8 grammar, and it is the one thing no source read can answer.

principles_to_propose.principle: A redundant layer is rarely ONLY redundant — before deleting a surface because it repeats, ledger every job it does, and give each unduplicated job a named destination before the delete lands.
principles_to_propose.rationale: This review's headline. The Fernwood tile row genuinely duplicated its summary text — and was simultaneously the sole above-fold door to four cards, the host of the loop's invitation, and the only place domains sat close enough to compare. All three were invisible from the angle that made the redundancy obvious. The authoring test is cheap: list what the surface DOES, not what it SAYS, and check each item against the surface you are folding it into. ⚠️ 1 occurrence, agent-proposed, NOT Paul's words.

principles_to_propose.principle: A closed/collapsed summary answers 'is there anything new behind this door?', never 'what is this card about?' — and a line that would render identically thirty days from now is furniture, not a summary.
principles_to_propose.rationale: F8. Operationalises Paul's 2026-09-04/09-07 empty ruling and his 2026-08-04 'furniture' word, and adds the piece both were missing: a mechanically checkable falsifier (render the resolver at today+30 and compare). Also supplies the degradation ladder — live line → dated change → character line → absence — so 'what does a collapsed card say' has one answer instead of the five vocabularies measured on one screen today. ⚠️ 1 occurrence, agent-proposed. Overlaps my earlier candidate from this morning ('a resolver with nothing to say returns null'); if Paul words one, he should word them as one rule.

principles_to_propose.principle: Distributing a synthesis destroys its ranking AND its adjacency — and the adjacency is the larger loss, because it is the comparison the reader was doing for free.
principles_to_propose.rationale: SECOND OCCURRENCE, with a sharpening, of the candidate I proposed this morning. That version named ranking. This pass measured the actual geometry: eight cells in one visual field become sixteen faces no two of which are ever on screen together at A+, so the reader loses not only the machine's ranking but her own eye's comparison. Pairs with the ratified 'Juxtapose large differences' — a gap the eye must cross costs precision, and here the gap becomes a scroll. ⚠️ Both occurrences are the same project and the same week, so I would NOT promote on this alone; watch for it outside Fernwood.

principles_to_propose.principle: An inferred ranking may PROPOSE a reader's order; it may never REPLACE an order the reader declared.
principles_to_propose.rationale: F9. The sharp corollary to the ratified 'A menu's order is a PLACE; a worklist's order is a RANKING.' That rule says do not let a ranking set an index. This one covers the case where the index order was authored BY THE USER — at which point overwriting it is not just a recall cost, it is the app contradicting a sentence it says on screen ('You put Gardening first'). The honest move is always propose-and-ratify, which also makes 'everything is changeable' true rather than asserted. ⚠️ 1 occurrence, agent-proposed.
